problem: Semantic navigation needs an ontology-based environment model plus a reasoner, but prior systems (e.g. NeoClassic/LOOM rule-based description logic) are hand-coded, and it is unclear which reasoning technology (relational database vs. a full knowledge-processing framework such as KnowRob) suits navigation.
motivation: Robots in human environments need high-level concepts (rooms, objects, utilities, meanings) to plan routes toward semantic goals such as 'go somewhere to work'. Reasoner choice affects execution time, ease of defining new environments, and scalability, so the paper compares two implementations of the same ontology.
key_idea: Implement the same object-room-utility-meaning ontology in two reasoners (SQL relational database vs. KnowRob/OWL/Prolog) behind a common Reasoner interface and compare them on output equivalence, query time, and a TurtleBot navigation demo.
insight: Both reasoners return identical inferences (only result ordering differs), so the choice is an engineering trade-off. The SQL reasoner is much faster (about 8.9% of KnowRob's time, ~11x faster, at 2-4 ms vs 16-63 ms per query, averaged over 100 runs) and easier to set up for new environments. KnowRob scales the ontology more easily and suits general cognitive reasoning. The experiments use a very small knowledge base, so the timing generalization is untested.
method: Ontology model: four entities (Conceptual Room, Conceptual Object, Physical Room, Physical Object) plus Interaction, utility and meaning relations, linking a conceptual hierarchy with a spatial hierarchy.
SQL-based reasoner: entity-relationship model mapped to tables (with join tables for many-to-many relations); inferences obtained through predefined SQL queries/views.

KnowRob-based reasoner: ontology authored in Protégé 5.1 as an OWL file (concept tree via is-a, relations via properties/restrictions such as contain), plus a separate OWL file for physical rooms/objects, queried via a ROS server running SWI-Prolog 6.6.
Common Reasoner interface: BDReasoner and KRReasoner both subclass a generic Reasoner class, so the semantic navigator, planner and explorer use them interchangeably.
Test program: runs every reasoner method (12 queries) on both backends, checks output equality, and averages execution time over 100 repetitions.

Robot demo: TurtleBot builds a geometric map with GMapping; the planner recursively chains reasoner answers, re-querying when the user rejects a result, to reach semantic goals (e.g. 'work' -> office, 'soft drink' -> kitchen).

setting.backbone: Ontology reasoners: SQL relational database vs. KnowRob (OWL + SWI-Prolog); no learned model
setting.observation: Laser-based 2D geometric map from GMapping on TurtleBot; semantic knowledge is prior, hand-entered
setting.action_space: High-level semantic goal -> target room/place, executed by standard ROS navigation
setting.privileged: Hand-crafted ontology and known physical instances (2 rooms, 5 instances) provided in advance

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark results; only a reasoner query-time comparison table (DB 2-4 ms vs KnowRob 16-63 ms) and a qualitative real-robot demo.
results: Both reasoners give identical outputs on 12 queries; the DB reasoner takes on average 8.9% of KnowRob's query time (about 11.13x faster; 2-4 ms vs 16-63 ms). The TurtleBot successfully reached the office for 'work' and the kitchen for 'soft drink' using the semantic reasoner.
limitations: Tiny knowledge base (2 rooms, 5 physical instances, 8 concepts), so timing and scalability claims are not tested on large ontologies.
Qualitative comparison rests on user experience, and the robot demo is anecdotal, with no navigation metrics (SR/SPL) or baselines.
The SQL views must be built by hand, and the KnowRob ontology is environment-specific and needs Protégé expertise.
builds_on: Crespo et al. SQL-based semantic reasoner (2015, 2017)
compares_to: KnowRob reasoner vs. SQL relational database reasoner
